		<item>
		<title>Compressing An 11B VLM To 2.7-bit Weights For Mobile CPUs</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/compressing-an-11b-vlm-to-2-7-bit-weights-for-mobile-cpus/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/compressing-an-11b-vlm-to-2-7-bit-weights-for-mobile-cpus/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Jeevan Bhoot]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 07:03:29 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[At The Core]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ARM]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CPUs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[LLMs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Mobile]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[multimodal]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[VLMs]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281447</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Combining a novel weight format for efficient decoding with quantization-aware training to reduce model size while retaining accuracy for multimodal AI.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/compressing-an-11b-vlm-to-2-7-bit-weights-for-mobile-cpus/">Compressing An 11B VLM To 2.7-bit Weights For Mobile CPUs</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As multimodal AI moves from the cloud to personal devices, developers face a fundamental constraint. Capable vision-language models require far more memory and bandwidth than most mobile systems can provide.</p>
<p>Mobile phones are a natural place to run multimodal AI. They already have cameras, microphones, sensors, and personal context on a single device. Running models locally also reduces reliance on cloud services, helping keep personal data on-device while reducing latency and improving responsiveness.</p>
<p>The challenge is fitting a model with billions of parameters within the memory and power constraints of a mobile device. Llama 3.2 Vision 11B needs 21.3 GB for its bfloat16 weights alone. Even with 4-bit quantization, the weights still require more than 5 GB. Reducing that footprint introduces two significant challenges. Developers need to preserve useful model accuracy and ensure that the target hardware can decode the compressed weights efficiently.</p>
<p>Llama-Mobile, developed by Graphcore Research in collaboration with Arm, introduces two key ideas:</p>
<ul>
<li>S3D8, a novel 2.7-bit weight format for efficient decoding on Arm CPUs</li>
<li>Quantization-aware training that does not require the model&#8217;s original training data</li>
</ul>
<p>Applied to Llama 3.2 Vision 11B, the approach reduces the weight footprint by more than 80%, from 21.3 GB to 3.7 GB. It also quantizes activations to INT8 while retaining an average visual question-answering score of 66.1%, compared with 74.4% for the original bfloat16 model.</p>
<h2>Designing a low-bit format around Arm SIMD</h2>
<p>S3D8 is a vector quantization format that stores 3 weights in a single byte, resulting in an average of 2.7 bits per parameter. Each byte contains a shared 5-bit centroid index and 1 sign bit for each weight. The index selects one of 32 learned centroids, stored as a 32&#215;3 table of positive INT8 values. A bfloat16 scale for each output channel preserves the weight range.</p>
<p>S3D8 is a compact storage format, not a new arithmetic format. During inference, Arm Advanced SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data), also known as Arm Neon, decodes multiple S3D8 values in parallel. It uses table-lookup instructions to convert the values into channel-scaled INT8. The CPU processes those weights using existing INT8 matrix multiplication instructions.</p>
<p>Separating storage from computation reduces memory traffic without requiring dedicated 2.7-bit arithmetic hardware.</p>
<h2>Matrix multiplication throughput on Google Pixel 8a</h2>
<p>Autoregressive token generation processes one token at a time, requiring the model weights to be read for each new token. This makes generation memory-bandwidth-bound, which is where the more compact S3D8 representation provides its clearest advantage over INT8, as shown in Table 1.</p>
<p>Text prefill and vision encoding process many tokens or patches at once. These operations are compute-bound: S3D8 must be decoded to INT8, so it performs similarly to INT8.</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">
<tbody>
<tr style="background-color: #ddd;">
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Pixel 8a workload</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>bfloat16 GMAC/s</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>INT8 GMAC/s</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>S3D8 GMAC/s</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Token generation</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">13.6</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">26.5</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">33.8</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Text prefill</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">76.3</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">201.1</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">197.7</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Vision encoding</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">116.5</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">206.1</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">211.8</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Table 1: Throughput for selected matrix multiplication operations in Llama 3.2 Vision 11B on five Pixel 8a CPU cores. </strong></p>
<p>For the token-generation workload, S3D8 reaches 33.8 GMAC/s, approximately 28% higher throughput than INT8 in this test. For the more compute-intensive prefill and vision workloads, S3D8 performance remains close to INT8.</p>
<p>Using a custom C++ runtime, the S3D8 quantized model generates a median 3.8 tokens per second on the Pixel 8a, excluding model loading and prefill.</p>
<h2>Recovering accuracy with quantization-aware distillation</h2>
<p>Llama-Mobile uses quantization-aware training (QAT) to recover much of the accuracy lost from quantizing weights to less than 3 bits. Specifically, it uses quantization-aware distillation (QAD), where a quantized student learns from the original bfloat16 teacher model.</p>
<p>During fine-tuning, the student uses quantized weights and INT8 activations in the forward pass while learning to match the teacher’s next-token distribution. This approach exposes the model to quantization effects during training rather than applying compression only after training is complete.</p>
<p>A practical challenge with QAT is obtaining suitable fine-tuning data. The datasets used to train the original model are often unavailable. Llama-Mobile addresses this challenge by creating a synthetic dataset. The teacher model generates responses for images sampled from ImageNet, and the resulting image-text examples are then used to fine-tune the quantized student.</p>
<p>This distillation approach avoids dependence on the original model-training corpus, which may be proprietary, inaccessible, or too costly to reproduce.</p>
<p>Figure 1 compares QAT with direct casting and GPTQ. Direct casting maps each weight to its nearest quantized value without calibration or training. GPTQ is a post-training quantization method that uses calibration data and second-order information to reduce quantization error.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281449" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?resize=1279%2C894&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1279" height="894" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?w=1279&amp;ssl=1 1279w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C210&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C716&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C537&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arm_Compressing-VLM-for-mobile-CPUs-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C419&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Average performance across VQAv2, ChartQA, DocVQA, and AI2D across bit widths. Direct cast and QAT use INT8 activations, while GPTQ is weight-only with bfloat16 activations.</strong></p>
<p>Direct-cast task performance degrades sharply below 4 bits per parameter, falling below 40% at around 3.5 bits. GPTQ retains more accuracy across the sweep, but QAT performs best under extreme compression.</p>
<p>At approximately 2.7 bits per parameter, S3D8 with GPTQ scores 34%, compared with 1.8% for rate-matched INT with GPTQ. Both results use the same quantization method, so the comparison isolates the benefit of the S3D8 representation.</p>
<p>Applying QAT to S3D8 increases the score to 66.1%, compared to 74.4% for the original bfloat16 model. Quantization-aware training recovers most of the accuracy that would otherwise be lost at this bit width.</p>
<h2>What Llama-Mobile shows for edge inference on Arm CPUs</h2>
<p>Llama-Mobile shows how an 11B parameter VLM can be compressed for an Arm mobile CPU. S3D8 reduces the model weights from 21.3 GB to 3.7 GB. With QAT, the model retains an average task score of 66.1%, compared with 74.4% for the original model.</p>
<p>For Arm CPU developers, the key takeaway is the value of flexible weight formats that separate storage from computation. S3D8 stores weights compactly at 2.7 bits per parameter, then decodes them into INT8 values for use with existing matrix multiplication instructions. This approach reduces memory traffic without requiring dedicated low-bit arithmetic support.</p>
<p>S3D8 also demonstrates the benefit of designing a quantization format around the target hardware. The layout works efficiently with Arm Advanced SIMD table-lookup instructions, enabling fast parallel decoding during inference. The result is higher throughput during memory-bandwidth-bound token generation, while maintaining performance similar to INT8 for compute-bound workloads such as text prefill.</p>
<p>The broader lesson extends beyond one model or quantization format. As edge AI systems become more capable, practical deployment will increasingly depend on co-design. This includes model architecture, numerical representation, software kernels, and processor capabilities.</p>
<p>This study covers just one VLM, but it demonstrates a practical approach to multimodal inference at the edge. Future work can explore how the same principles apply to different model sizes and architectures, device classes, Arm CPU generations, and multimodal workloads. This work could expand the range of AI experiences that can run privately and responsively on-device.</p>
<p>Ready to go deeper? Explore how Llama-Mobile was built, benchmarked, and trained, including the full technical methodology and implementation details, in the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21134">Llama-Mobile paper</a> and <a href="https://graphcore-research.github.io/2026-08-24-llama-mobile/">Graphcore Research blog</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/compressing-an-11b-vlm-to-2-7-bit-weights-for-mobile-cpus/">Compressing An 11B VLM To 2.7-bit Weights For Mobile CPUs</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Validating PCIe 6.0 Connectivity In A 3D Multi-Die Test Chip</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/validating-pcie-6-0-connectivity-in-a-3d-multi-die-test-chip/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/validating-pcie-6-0-connectivity-in-a-3d-multi-die-test-chip/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Madhumita Sanyal]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 07:02:24 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IP And LP In SoCs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Implementing 64.0 GT/s PCIe connectivity in a stacked-die, face-to-face 3D architecture. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/validating-pcie-6-0-connectivity-in-a-3d-multi-die-test-chip/">Validating PCIe 6.0 Connectivity In A 3D Multi-Die Test Chip</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI, high-performance computing (HPC), data center switching, and storage systems are increasing the amount of data that must move across interfaces and between heterogeneous dies, or chiplets. That demand is exposing limits in traditional monolithic system-on-chip (SoC) architectures. Synopsys’ 3D PCIe 6.0 test-chip demonstration shows that 64.0 GT/s PCIe connectivity, with up to 128.0 GB/s delivered through an 8-lane configuration using PAM4 signaling, can be implemented and validated in a stacked-die, face-to-face 3D architecture rather than only in a conventional 2D design.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281436" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=624%2C624&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="624" height="624" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?w=624&amp;ssl=1 624w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C300&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=150%2C150&amp;ssl=1 150w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C600&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=100%2C100&amp;ssl=1 100w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=24%2C24&amp;ssl=1 24w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=48%2C48&amp;ssl=1 48w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Validating-PCIe-6-3D-Multi-Die-fig1.webp?resize=96%2C96&amp;ssl=1 96w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 624px) 100vw, 624px" /></p>
<p><strong>Linear transmitter eyes and receiver eyes at 64 GT/s exceeding PCIe 6.0 BER requirements by multiple orders of magnitude.</strong></p>
<h2>3D PCIe 6.0 test-chip demonstration</h2>
<p>3D multi-die design offers a path to higher bandwidth, tighter coupling, and improved efficiency by reducing interconnect distance between dies. In 2.5D packaging, dies are placed side by side and connected through interposers; in 3D packaging, dies are stacked vertically to shorten interconnect distance and enable tighter coupling between heterogeneous functions.</p>
<p>The test chip for the 5-nm PCIe 6.0 PHY, with design updates for 3D-IC technology, is built on an existing PCIe 6.0 test-chip implementation. The excellent silicon results confirm that high-speed PCIe 6.0 IP can be adapted, packaged, brought up, and measured in a 3D environment, an increasingly necessary requirement as customers move from monolithic SoCs to multi-die designs. This enables homogeneous and heterogeneous die integration for high performance, high compute density, energy efficiency, low latency, higher integration, smaller form factors, better power and signal integrity, and lower power consumption compared with current state-of-the-art packaging approaches. The achievement is not just the PCIe 6.0 eye or loopback result in isolation, but the connection between 64 GT/s PCIe behavior, 3D packaging, validation infrastructure, and customer system requirements for AI, HPC, data center switching, and storage. Synopsys’ PCIe 6.0 at 64 GT/s, along with 3D-ready implementation expertise, helps customers design AI accelerators, HPC processors, data center switches, SmartNICs, DPUs, SSD controllers, and CXL-enabled systems with compact form factor.</p>
<h2>PCIe 6.0 implementation challenges in 3D packaging</h2>
<p>This 3D implementation introduced several challenges, including 3D PHY architectural analysis, TSV implementation and dummy die strategies to optimize performance, accurate modeling of interactions between the top and bottom dies, full-stack modeling and verification of inductor implementation, and minimizing added TSVs while meeting PCIe 6.0 performance goals.</p>
<p>This milestone reinforces Synopsys’ long PCIe legacy, including more than two decades of expertise, silicon-proven PHYs, digital controllers, IDE security IP, verification IP, and extensive third-party interoperability testing, covering hundreds of PCIe 6.x implementations and approximately 4,000 customer tape-outs across seven generations of PCI Express. The results demonstrate a path from standards leadership to mature PCIe IP, 3D-aware implementation, and silicon success. They also connect the proven PCIe ecosystem with emerging multi-die design architectures and give customers designing the next generation of AI infrastructure, HPC platforms, storage systems, and data center fabrics a clearer path for high-performance connectivity into 3D packaging without sacrificing the validation discipline, interoperability experience, and IP completeness that modern systems require.</p>
<p>As a trusted partner, Synopsys is driving the industry&#8217;s transformation to multi-die designs with a comprehensive and scalable solution for fast heterogeneous integration. The solution, including EDA and IP products, enables early architecture exploration, rapid software development and system validation, efficient multi-die/advanced package co-design and optimization with multi-physics analysis, robust die-to-die and chip-to-chip connectivity, and improved manufacturing and reliability.</p>

		<item>
		<title>One Processor, One Toolchain</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/one-processor-one-toolchain/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/one-processor-one-toolchain/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Steve Roddy]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 07:01:24 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Embedded ML Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[GPNPU]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[NPU]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Quadric]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281431</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>A single, software-controlled core that handles matrix, vector, and scalar code in one execution pipeline.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/one-processor-one-toolchain/">One Processor, One Toolchain</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Ask anyone who has shipped an edge-AI SoC where the schedule actually went sideways, and you&#8217;ll rarely hear &#8220;the math was wrong.&#8221; What you&#8217;ll hear about is the <strong>bring-up</strong>: the week spent reconciling three debuggers, the accuracy bug that turned out to be a silent fallback between two cores, the handoff that worked in simulation and stalled in silicon.</p>
<p>That pain isn&#8217;t bad luck, it&#8217;s the predictable and direct result of an architecture that splits one workload across three different processors and forces the developer to try and make them dance together. The solution isn&#8217;t a better debugger for each core, it&#8217;s not needing three cores in the first place.</p>
<h2>The conventional stack: Three engines</h2>
<p>A typical AI SoC routes work to whichever processor suits each job: control logic runs on the CPU, signal processing runs on the DSP, and neural inference runs on the NPU. On paper, each core does what it does best, but in practice, getting them to play nice becomes half the project.</p>
<p>The problem is structural. As one industry survey of heterogeneous architectures put it, neural networks aren&#8217;t programmed, they&#8217;re trained, while DSPs and CPUs are written in C and C++ with a traditional IDE and debugger. Three processor types means three programming models, three toolchains, three binary formats, and a different debugger for each.</p>
<p>What the bring-up team actually inherits is this mess:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Toolchain fragmentation:</strong> Each core needs its own compiler, its own binary format, and its own debug tools.</li>
<li><strong>Cross-core synchronization:</strong> Halting all three engines together requires a hardware cross-trigger network just to stop the clock coherently.</li>
<li><strong>Silent operator fallbacks:</strong> When one engine hits an unsupported operator, work quietly reverts to another core. It stalls the pipeline, conceals the root cause, and cripples performance.</li>
<li><strong>Shared-memory contention:</strong> Bandwidth fights between cores produce timing bugs that vanish the moment you attach a debugger.</li>
</ul>
<p>None of these are exotic, they&#8217;re the standard tax on splitting one application across three engines. And that tax compounds: every new accelerator on the next chip adds another toolchain, another binary, and another debug context.</p>
<p>The orchestration layer that routes work and coordinates cores has become the defining engineering challenge of embedded AI software. That is a problem worth deleting, not optimizing.</p>
<h2>One core, one program, one toolchain</h2>
<p>Quadric&#8217;s Chimera is a <strong>GPNPU</strong>, a general-purpose neural processing unit. The architecture is a single, software-controlled core that handles matrix, vector, and scalar code in one execution pipeline; work that conventionally requires an NPU, a DSP, and a real-time CPU runs on one engine instead of three.</p>
<p>That single design decision removes the seams. There&#8217;s no partition to negotiate because there&#8217;s only one processor in the first place. You don&#8217;t have to debug the handoff if there&#8217;s no handoff. You have one toolchain and one target. If you run control DSP and ML code merged on one processor, there&#8217;s no need to artificially partition your application.</p>
<p>The developer experience follows from the hardware. Models import through the Chimera Graph Compiler from standard formats like ONNX. Anything without a standard equivalent — a custom operator, a bespoke pre-processing step — is written in <strong>standard C++</strong> against the same compute library, compiled by the same toolchain, and debugged in the same environment as everything else. DSP code and ML code aren&#8217;t two worlds bridged by glue, they&#8217;re one program.</p>
<h3>Same workload, two development realities</h3>
<p>The contrast is sharpest when you line up what each approach asks the developer to manage.</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">
<thead>
<tr style="background-color: #ddd;">
<td style="padding: 5px;">What you manage</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">CPU + DSP + NPU</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Chimera GPNPU</td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Processors to integrate</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Three separate cores</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">One unified core</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Toolchains</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Three (C/C++ IDE, DSP tools, NN compiler)</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">One, the Chimera SDK</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Binary formats</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Three, all different</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">One</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Debuggers</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">One per core + cross-trigger sync</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">One</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Code partitioning</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Manual, by hand</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">None: write one program</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Operator fallbacks</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">Silent reverts between cores</td>
<td style="padding: 5px;">No cross-core handoff</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>That table is a list of problems that just don&#8217;t exist on the Chimera GPNPU. There&#8217;s no partitioning step risking partitioning bugs, there&#8217;s no format reconciliation because there&#8217;s only one binary format, and there&#8217;s no cross-trigger choreography to manage. You just need a single debugger. The problem never happens because the architecture already solved it.</p>
<h2>Why the simplicity is structural, not cosmetic</h2>
<p>It&#8217;s fair to ask whether this approach just shifts the complexity somewhere else, like the compiler. It doesn&#8217;t, and here&#8217;s why:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>A unified ISA means one mental model.</strong> Engineers reason about one instruction stream, one memory view, and one set of tools instead of three that must be kept consistent with each other.</li>
<li><strong>No inter-core handoff means an entire class of bugs disappears.</strong> Silent fallbacks, lockstep-debug metastability, and cross-core synchronization vanish when there&#8217;s only one core to begin with.</li>
<li><strong>One toolchain means one team.</strong> The DSP specialists, the ML engineers, and the firmware developers work in the same environment instead of meeting only at the integration boundary, where conventional schedules slip.</li>
<li><strong>Full programmability means durability.</strong> Because every operator – both current and future &#8211; is expressible in C++, a model that introduces a new operator next year does not strand the silicon. The same toolchain compiles it.</li>
</ul>
<p>The conventional stack treats heterogeneity as a feature and pays for it at integration time. Chimera treats the integration cost as the thing to eliminate, and delivers the heterogeneity — scalar, vector, and matrix compute — inside a single programmable core.</p>
<h2>Maybe just have the one toolchain</h2>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281432" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Quadric_One-Processor-One-Toolchain-fig1.webp?resize=624%2C341&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="624" height="341" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Quadric_One-Processor-One-Toolchain-fig1.webp?w=624&amp;ssl=1 624w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Quadric_One-Processor-One-Toolchain-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C164&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Quadric_One-Processor-One-Toolchain-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C328&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 624px) 100vw, 624px" /></p>
<p>Debugging across a CPU, a DSP, and an NPU is hard because it&#8217;s really three debugging problems standing on each other&#8217;s shoulders and wearing a trench coat. The toolchains, the binaries, the cross-core synchronization, and the silent fallbacks are all a direct consequence of the partition. Remove the partition and you remove the problems.</p>
<p>The Chimera GPNPU makes a very convincing argument: that the cleanest way to debug three chains is to just&#8230; not have to in the first place. Maybe just do the one instead.</p>
<p>Learn more about the Chimera GPNPU and the Chimera SDK at <a href="https://quadric.ai">quadric.ai</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/one-processor-one-toolchain/">One Processor, One Toolchain</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>How to understand every chiplet inside the system-in-package.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/advanced-packaging-changes-the-rules-for-semiconductor-health-and-performance-management/">Advanced Packaging Changes The Rules For Semiconductor Health And Performance Management</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Systems-in-Package (SiPs) are enabling the next generation of Agentic and Physical AI across cloud, telecommunications, mobile, automotive and high-performance computing platforms. As infrastructure evolves from monolithic devices toward heterogeneous architectures, advanced packaging is becoming increasingly critical to achieving the required performance, bandwidth and power efficiency. But as processors, accelerators, memory and connectivity are brought together through increasingly sophisticated multi-die packages, managing each component in isolation is no longer enough.</p>
<p>A SiP is not simply a collection of individual dies. Once chiplets are integrated into the same package, new interactions emerge between them and with the package itself. Understanding those interactions requires visibility not only into each individual chiplet, but into how the chiplets behave together as a system.</p>
<h2>Why a SiP is harder than the sum of its dies</h2>
<p>Advanced packaging enables semiconductor companies to integrate more dies and increasingly heterogeneous components using technologies such as interposers, advanced substrates, through-silicon vias (TSVs), die stacking and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). These architectures provide enormous benefits, but they also introduce new electrical, thermal and mechanical interactions.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281159" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig1.webp?resize=828%2C323&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="828" height="323" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig1.webp?w=828&amp;ssl=1 828w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C117&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C300&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C234&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 828px) 100vw, 828px" /></p>
<p><strong>Challenges of systems-in-package.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Power delivery becomes a system-level challenge.</strong> Different chiplets can have very different power demands, and activity on one die can influence the operating margins of another. IR drop, simultaneous switching noise, fast transients and shared power delivery networks can create voltage behavior that cannot be understood by looking at each chiplet independently.</p>
<p><strong>Thermal behavior becomes increasingly coupled.</strong> High-power compute dies, HBM and other components are placed in close proximity, creating hotspots, thermal gradients and heat transfer between neighboring dies. In 3D architectures, heat removal becomes even more difficult as dies are vertically stacked and thermal paths become constrained.</p>
<p><strong>Mechanical effects can become electrical effects.</strong> Warpage, package stress and thermo-mechanical effects introduced during assembly can alter timing and voltage margins. A die that behaved one way at wafer sort may behave differently after it has been bonded, stacked or integrated into the final package.</p>
<p><strong>Yield economics become more challenging.</strong> A marginal die discovered at wafer sort is one problem. Discovering that same die after it has been integrated with an expensive interposer, substrate, HBM and other known-good components is a much more costly problem. Compound yield therefore becomes increasingly important as the number and value of components within the package increase.</p>
<p>And <strong>observability becomes harder just when it becomes more important.</strong> Once dies are assembled into a package, traditional probing becomes limited, fault isolation becomes more difficult and determining whether a problem originated in a chiplet, an interface, the package or an interaction between components can require significant debug effort.</p>
<p><strong>Quality becomes harder to measure and assure.</strong> Advanced packaging introduces thousands of critical connections, including micro-bumps and other package interconnects, whose quality can be difficult to characterize directly. Marginal connections may pass conventional production tests yet contribute to degradation or failures later in the product lifecycle. When a system fails in production or returns from the field, determining whether the root cause lies in the chiplets, an interconnect or the package itself can be extremely difficult. This creates a need for measurable indicators of quality that can help identify marginalities early and track degradation over time.</p>
<p><strong>Power delivery is one important example.</strong> As power traverses increasingly complex package structures and interconnects, and as the current density over these structures is ever increasing, the quality of the power-delivery path can directly affect voltage margin and system behavior. Different chiplets can have very different power demands, while IR drop, simultaneous switching noise, fast transients and shared power delivery networks can create effects that cannot be understood by looking at each chiplet independently. Even though power delivery is distributed over thousands of bumps, pads and through silicon vias (TSVs), a degradation of even one of them may cause a domino effect causing faster degradation of the neighboring pads.</p>
<p>The challenge is amplified further as the industry moves toward heterogeneous, multi-vendor chiplet ecosystems. No single die tells the whole story – and no single chiplet vendor necessarily has visibility into the complete package.</p>
<h2>Shift left: Know more before you package</h2>
<p>The economics of advanced packaging make early decisions particularly valuable.</p>
<p>Conventional pass/fail testing at wafer sort may not reveal the parametric marginalities that become important after integration. For advanced packaging, that may not be enough. A die can pass conventional tests and still carry parametric marginalities that become important only after packaging.</p>
<p>Deep in-die measurements can provide another layer of information: how much timing margin exists, how a die responds to voltage variation, whether its parametric signature differs from its population and whether its behavior indicates increased sensitivity to the conditions it will experience after assembly.</p>
<p>This enables manufacturers to shift critical decisions left, before committing a die to an increasingly valuable package.</p>
<p>For example, telemetry-based advanced analytics and parametric deep data at wafer sort enable outlier detection beyond the industry’s best known methods, per-chiplet VDDmin prediction for static Voperational setting, and power/performance grading for chiplet mix-and-match. These insights can increase confidence in known-good-die quality and help prevent marginal dies from progressing into expensive downstream assembly.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281160" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=2190%2C1120&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2190" height="1120" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?w=2190&amp;ssl=1 2190w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C153&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C524&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C393&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=1536%2C786&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=2048%2C1047&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C307&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Advanced telemetry-based analytics for shift-left SiP production testing. </strong></p>
<p>The objective is no longer simply <strong>Known Good Die</strong>. It is increasingly:</p>
<p><strong>Is this die ready to become part of this SiP?</strong></p>
<p>That distinction can have a significant impact on compound yield, package scrap cost and final product quality.</p>
<h2>What changed throughout packaging?</h2>
<p>Pre-packaging visibility is only one side of the problem.</p>
<p>Once a die has been integrated, manufacturers need to understand what has changed.</p>
<p>This is where <strong>pre-to-post packaging correlation</strong> becomes particularly valuable. By comparing parametric behavior before and after integration, changes associated with packaging can be identified and quantified.</p>
<p>A shift in timing margin, for example, may indicate an integration-induced effect rather than an intrinsic silicon defect. Changes in voltage behavior may point toward package power delivery. Spatial or die-to-die differences may correlate with thermal gradients, warpage or structural stress.</p>
<p>This becomes especially important across advanced packaging technologies such as interposers, substrates, HBM and TSV-based 3D stacks.</p>
<p>Instead of asking only:</p>
<p><strong>“Does the assembled SiP pass?”</strong></p>
<p>manufacturers can begin asking:</p>
<p><strong>“What parameters changed when we packaged it? And why?”</strong></p>
<p>That provides a much richer basis for package characterization, guard-band definition, root-cause analysis and production decisions.</p>
<h2>From individual dies to synchronized inter-chiplet analysis</h2>
<p>Post-packaging, the SiP increasingly needs to be treated as a system in its own right.</p>
<p>The behavior of one chiplet can affect another. A workload on a compute die can change package power demand, influence voltage droops, generate additional heat and affect timing margins elsewhere in the package. These interactions may also be transient, making static measurements insufficient.</p>
<p>Synchronized inter-chiplet analysis addresses this problem by analyzing measurements from multiple dies simultaneously and over time.</p>
<p>This enables engineers to correlate events across chiplets and investigate questions such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>Did a timing-margin shift on one chiplet coincide with a power event on another?</li>
<li>Is a high temperature in one chiplet affecting the margin of a neighboring chiplet?</li>
<li>Does a particular workload trigger correlated voltage or clock noise across multiple chiplets?</li>
<li>Is an observed anomaly intrinsic to one die, or caused by an interaction within the package?</li>
</ul>
<p>Time-series analysis adds another dimension by revealing transient instability and workload-dependent behavior that may not appear in static test results.</p>
<p>The result is a transition from <strong>per-chip monitoring</strong> toward <strong>package-aware analysis</strong>.</p>
<h2>Multiple data streams, one view of the SiP</h2>
<p>Advanced packaging also increases the number of relevant data sources.</p>
<p>Measurements originate from proteanTecs’ embedded monitors and sensors across multiple chiplets, in combination with manufacturing test equipment data and other third-party sources. Looking at these streams independently can miss the relationships between them.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281161" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig3.webp?resize=505%2C479&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="505" height="479" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig3.webp?w=505&amp;ssl=1 505w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C285&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig3.webp?resize=24%2C24&amp;ssl=1 24w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 505px) 100vw, 505px" /></p>
<p><strong>Example: Multi-die monitoring on proteanTecs’ <a href="https://www.proteantecs.com/blog/systemlens-gives-system-engineers-real-time-visibility-into-hidden-silicon-issues-under-functional-tests">SystemLens</a>.</strong></p>
<p>Multi-stream analytics synchronizes and combines these measurements in the context of the complete SiP, allowing timing, voltage and thermal behavior to be correlated across chiplets, test stages and workload conditions.</p>
<p>This is particularly valuable when determining whether a problem originates in silicon, assembly, package power delivery, thermal interaction or workload behavior.</p>
<h2>3D integration raises the stakes further</h2>
<p>Many of these challenges become even more pronounced in 3D architectures.</p>
<p>Vertical stacking introduces additional dependencies around TSV integrity, thermo-mechanical stress, heat removal and vertical power delivery. It also creates the concept of a <strong>Known-Good-Stack (KGS)</strong> <strong>for 3D architectures</strong>, in addition to the traditional Known-Good-Die.</p>
<p>Testing and monitoring therefore need to move progressively through the stack lifecycle.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281162" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig4.webp?resize=336%2C254&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="336" height="254" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig4.webp?w=336&amp;ssl=1 336w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig4.webp?resize=300%2C227&amp;ssl=1 300w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 336px) 100vw, 336px" /></p>
<p>Before final packaging, stack-level testing helps identify interface issues, thermo-mechanical effects and TSV integrity problems. At final test, the fully assembled package can be validated under realistic conditions. During operation, the same embedded visibility can support monitoring of interface degradation and stack reliability over time.</p>
<p>The ability to maintain visibility through these stages becomes increasingly valuable because physical access decreases as integration increases.</p>
<h2>From production visibility to in-mission awareness</h2>
<p>The interactions created by advanced packaging do not stop when a SiP passes production test.</p>
<p>Workloads change. Temperatures change. Components age. And the guard-bands of different chiplets may evolve differently throughout the product lifetime. Interconnect quality can degrade as well. Continuous in-mission measurements can provide indicators of marginal or degrading package connections, helping distinguish interconnect-related issues from silicon, thermal or power-delivery effects when failures emerge over time. In-mission health and performance management therefore needs to become package-aware as well.</p>
<p>Thermal, power and timing awareness across the SiP can provide the context required to understand which chiplet is limiting system guard-bands at a particular point in time. Runtime applications can then use this information to support decisions around voltage, frequency, thermal management, health and reliability.</p>
<p>This is particularly important because SiP architectures can differ substantially. Some use centralized control through a primary chiplet; others distribute control functions. Power and clock domains may be shared or independent. Voltage regulators may be centralized or local, or even based on distributed Integrated Voltage Regulators (IVR) embedded into the package substrate.</p>
<p>There is no single control architecture for every SiP.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281163" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=1703%2C542&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1703" height="542" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?w=1703&amp;ssl=1 1703w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=300%2C95&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=1024%2C326&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=768%2C244&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=1536%2C489&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/proteanTecs_Adv-Pack-Changes-Rules-Semi-Health-Perf-Mgmt-fig5.webp?resize=600%2C191&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>proteanTecs select applications for in-field health management, power reduction, and performance optimization.</strong></p>
<p>Health management and power reduction (or performance increase) therefore needs to adapt to the architecture of the package while evaluating the behavior of the complete system.</p>
<h2>One continuous view across the SiP lifecycle</h2>
<p>The common thread across all of these challenges is visibility.</p>
<p>Before packaging, visibility helps determine whether a chiplet is truly ready for integration. After packaging, it helps determine what changed and how the chiplets are interacting. During production, it enables better screening, correlation, voltage setting and test decisions. And during in-mission operation, it provides the thermal, power, timing margin and health awareness required to optimize the complete SiP over its lifetime.</p>
<p>proteanTecs extends its deep data analytics and real-time health and performance monitoring and real time actuation capabilities across this lifecycle, combining an embedded <a href="https://www.proteantecs.com/blog/why-hardware-monitoring-needs-infrastructure-not-just-sensors">Hardware Monitoring System </a>with cloud, on-tester and real-time applications.</p>
<p>Together, these capabilities enable semiconductor and system companies to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Increase confidence in known-good-die and known-good-stack quality</li>
<li>Shift critical decisions earlier in the manufacturing flow</li>
<li>Improve visibility into package power delivery network and interconnect quality</li>
<li>Improve compound yield and reduce costly package scrap</li>
<li>Accelerate SiP characterization and root-cause analysis</li>
<li>Optimize power and performance across multi-die systems</li>
<li>Improve long-term health, reliability and lifecycle power/performance</li>
</ul>
<p>As the industry moves toward increasingly heterogeneous and sophisticated multi-die architectures, the fundamental question is changing.</p>
<p>It is no longer enough to know whether each die works.</p>
<p>You need to know how every die is behaving, and how they are behaving together.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/advanced-packaging-changes-the-rules-for-semiconductor-health-and-performance-management/">Advanced Packaging Changes The Rules For Semiconductor Health And Performance Management</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

<td style="padding: 12px 30px 18px 40px; border: 1px solid #14532D;"><strong>Dissecting the transition metal dichalcogenides-based metal-oxide-semiconductor structures charge components</strong> <sup><a href="https://semiengineering.com/characterizing-charge-components-in-tmd-based-mos-structures-imec-ku-leuven-asm/"><img src="https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f517.png" alt="🔗" class="wp-smiley" style="height: 1em; max-height: 1em;" /></a></sup></td>
<td style="padding: 12px 18px 18px 30px; border: 1px solid #14532D;"><strong>imec</strong>, <strong>KU Leuven</strong>, <strong>ASM</strong></td>
